references.text: Samuel hews down King Agag before the Lord—a judgment against God's enemy who refused to submit. The parallel to Luke 19:27 is clear: enemies who did not want this man to reign over them are executed in his presence. [ref:1 Sam 15:33|1 Samuel 15:33]
The psalm about the Messiah-King who will crush his enemies with a rod of iron—an image of the final judgment on those who rebel against God's anointed King. [ref:Ps 2:9|Psalm 2:9]
The Lord will swallow up his enemies in his wrath—an expression of God's judgment on those who stand against him, just as the king in the parable judges his enemies. [ref:Ps 21:9|Psalm 21:9]

The Lord says to the Messiah: "Sit at my right hand until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet." The king's enemies will be placed under his rule—the same theme as in the parable. [ref:Ps 110:1-2|Psalm 110:1-2]
The Lord's voice from the temple brings retribution to the enemies—a prophecy of God's final judgment on his opponents. [ref:Isa 66:6|Isaiah 66:6]

The background for verse 27: The citizens hated the new king and sent messengers with this message: "We do not want this man to reign over us." Verse 27 is the direct judgment on these enemies. [ref:Lk 19:14|Luke 19:14]

Jesus prophesies about the destruction of Jerusalem—that the people will fall by the edge of the sword—as a historical fulfillment of the judgment in the parable over those who rejected their king. [ref:Lk 21:24|Luke 21:24]

Paul writes about Jesus' return with punishing judgment on those who do not know God and are not obedient to the gospel—an eschatological parallel to the judgment on the king's enemies. [ref:2 Thess 1:8-9|2 Thessalonians 1:8-9]

The heavenly King, the Word from God, returns to strike down the nations and judge his enemies—the ultimate fulfillment of the parable's judgment on the enemies who did not want him to reign over them. [ref:Rev 19:11-15|Revelation 19:11-15]
